name: Venaz
tagline: An AI agent product that layers task automation and chat on top of foundation models.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: This is a thin-surface AI agent product, and the public detail on it is thin too, so treat this entry as a shape-level judgment rather than a teardown. The generic shape, a chat interface plus tool calling plus a bit of memory over someone else's model, is exactly the thing coding agents are good at reproducing in an afternoon. Where these products actually earn money is the boring part: the connectors into your real systems, the retries when a tool call fails, the permission model, and the fact that someone else is on the hook when it breaks. A personal build gets you the loop and the satisfaction, not the plumbing. If the real value here turns out to be a specific vertical dataset or a set of hard-won integrations, downgrade this to a no and move on.
coreLoopDIY: A local chat app that talks to a hosted LLM, calls a handful of tools you define, and remembers your past sessions in a local database.
requirements: An API key for a hosted model provider, billed to you
Willingness to write each integration by hand
whatYouLose: Prebuilt connectors to whatever SaaS you already use, plus the OAuth dances behind them
Someone else's evaluation and prompt tuning work, which is more of the quality than people admit
Hosting, background job execution, and anything that needs to run while your laptop is shut
A team-facing surface: shared workspaces, roles, audit trails
Support when the agent confidently does the wrong thing
moatNotes: For any agent wrapper, the moat is never the model. It is the connector list and the unglamorous error handling.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the demo of an agent and a dependable agent are separated by a few hundred edge cases nobody wants to own personally. Paying gets you connectors that already work, a runtime that keeps going when your machine sleeps, and a vendor to blame. The DIY version is genuinely useful for one person with three tools and patience, and genuinely miserable the moment you need it to run on a schedule for a team.
notes: Category-level verdict, not a considered review: the public surface here is too thin for anything sharper.
prompt:
Build a local-first AI agent workbench. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable: TypeScript, Node 20, Hono for the HTTP server, SQLite via better-sqlite3, and plain server-rendered HTML with htmx for the UI. No React, no build step, no Docker.

What it does:
1. A single-page chat UI at / with a message list, an input box, and a session sidebar.
2. Streams responses from one hosted LLM provider using the OpenAI-compatible chat completions API. Read OPENAI_API_KEY, OPENAI_BASE_URL and MODEL from .env. Ship a .env.example, never a real key.
3. Tool calling with a small registry in src/tools/. Implement exactly four tools: read_file and write_file scoped to a ./workspace directory, run_shell with a hardcoded allowlist of commands, and http_get. Every tool call is logged to SQLite with arguments, result, duration and error.
4. A tool call approval mode: if REQUIRE_APPROVAL=true, write_file and run_shell pause and wait for a click in the UI before executing.
5. Sessions and messages persist in SQLite so restarting the server loses nothing. Sidebar lists sessions with title, timestamp and token count.
6. A /runs page showing every tool call ever made, newest first, with the raw JSON expandable.
7. A per-session system prompt, editable in the UI and stored with the session.

Explicitly out of scope: multi-user auth, vector search, RAG, background scheduling, OAuth connectors, mobile.

Safety: run_shell refuses anything outside the allowlist, file tools reject paths escaping ./workspace, and both are covered by tests.

Deliver: README with setup in under five commands, npm run dev, npm test with vitest covering the tool sandbox and the SQLite persistence layer, and seed data so the UI is not empty on first run.
